newsitem.title: UK: The commodity markets end a turbulent year.
newsitem.headline: The commodity markets end a turbulent year.

text.p: Commodity prices ended a turbulent 1996 on Tuesday with oil riding high on the back of icy weather, wheat sharply below historic levels seen at mid-year and gold languishing in the bargain basement.

Coffee and cocoa also ended down from a year ago. So did copper, flagship of the industrial metals. But it has staged a vigorous recovery from a nosedive at the time of the Sumitomo scandal. Analysts expected that 1997 would also see the various commodity markets moving different ways, largely on the basis of their own fundamentals of supply, demand and stock levels. "The past year saw commodity markets as a whole move in a somewhat erratic trading pattern..." says brokerage Merrill Lynch in its Outlook For Global Commodity Markets.

Merrill sees a similar pattern at least for early on in the coming 12 months "with no broad based directional bias and few indications of any inflationary threats". Crude oil was the big 1996 winner, up an average $3 per barrel.

Low stocks and cold weather that fired up demand for heating fuel in North America and Europe drove crude oil to a post-Gulf War high above $25 in October. And the benchmark Brent Blend was ending the year almost at $24 despite the easing of the U.N. Gulf War embargo on Iraq.

Traders differ on how far demand may suffice to mop up extra Iraqi and other supply in 1997 and keep prices above $20. World grain stocks were depleted in 1996 to their lowest for 20 years after earlier droughts in Australia, Russia and North Africa. For several months the European Union suspended exports. In this tight market, bellwether Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures "spiked" to a record $7.50 per bushel.
But a subsequent harvest of bumper crops around the globe later took the heat out of prices. CBOT nearby wheat was down around $3.80 on Tuesday compared with $5 at the end of 1995.
Speculators ran out of patience with gold.

It began January at $386 for an ounce, struggled up to $416 in February then sank to its lowest value in three years at just under $370 in November. At its last London fixing on Tuesday morning it stood at $369.55.
It began 1996 on the London Metal Exchange (LME) at $2,658 per tonne and on May 8 touched $2,715.

Then, on June 14, Japanese metals conglomerate Sumitomo Corp said it had fired its head trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, alleging that he had turned out to be a maverick who had lost it $2.6 billion in 10 years of unauthorized deals.

Hamanaka had been the mastermind of the world trade in copper and, when sacked, was defending a long, high price position against waves of speculative selling. Copper crashed as low as $1,745 soon after his dismissal. But it has rebounded to end the year up above $2,100 because of low world stocks that barely suffice to cover a month's supply. Tight stocks also helped to bolster coffee in 1996.

But the London Robusta futures price fell as low as $1,225 this month after beginning the year at $1,755 and reaching a high in January at $2,175 on frost fears in Latin America. Lawrence Eagles, commodity analyst at brokerage GNI Ltd, says the market is still tight so that volatility may continue.
Cocoa and sugar also eased in 1996. London markets closed early on Tuesday ahead of the New Year holiday and reopen on Thursday.
